findings.body: Existing CryptoProvider implementations that do not implement order() fail to compile, and pre-compiled classes loaded via ServiceLoader without this method throw AbstractMethodError at runtime, breaking custom crypto provider integrations.
findings.failure_mode: Compile-time failure or AbstractMethodError for pre-existing CryptoProvider implementors.
findings.impact: Existing CryptoProvider implementations that do not implement order() fail to compile, and pre-compiled classes loaded via ServiceLoader without this method throw AbstractMethodError at runtime, breaking custom crypto provider integrations.
findings.root_cause: New abstract interface method added without a default implementation.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `default int order() { return 100; }` (or similar sensible default) to preserve backward compatibility, matching the pattern used for getSupportedKeyStoreTypes() elsewhere in this interface.
findings.title: New CryptoProvider.order() method breaks existing implementers
findings.trigger: Any existing third-party or in-repo implementation of the CryptoProvider interface (compiled against the old interface, or any future implementation that forgets to override order()) is compiled/loaded against this interface after the change.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch adds `int order();` at line 44 of CryptoProvider.java without a default implementation. The interface is public and loaded via ServiceLoader. Existing third-party implementations compiled against the old interface will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when order() is invoked during sorting in detectProvider(). The evidence shows multiple implementations exist (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, AuthzClientCryptoProvider) and the new method is called via `CryptoProvider::order` in CryptoIntegration.java:57.

findings.body: Two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to purely to be discarded, wasting allocations/CPU on every signature conversion and confusing maintainers into thinking they have an effect.
findings.failure_mode: Unnecessary object allocation and misleading dead code in a hot signing path.
findings.impact: Two ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to purely to be discarded, wasting allocations/CPU on every signature conversion and confusing maintainers into thinking they have an effect.
findings.root_cause: Leftover/duplicated code from development that was not cleaned up before submitting.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the two unused `ASN1Encoder.create().write(...)` statements; only the final writeDerSeq(...) chain is actually used.
findings.title: Dead/discarded ASN1Encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.trigger: Every call to concatenatedRSToASN1DER (i.e. every ECDSA signature produced by the authz-client) executes these two statements.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch lines R114-R115 show `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose return values are discarded. The actual encoding happens at R117-R121 with new ASN1Encoder instances. These two statements create objects, write to them, and discard them - confirmed dead code that wastes allocations.

pr.body:
…tory

closes #33831

This is the Keycloak main part for solving the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/32962 and adding the related changes in the authz-client on the Keycloak side, which can then be later synced to the keycloak-client repository. 

In the end, I am using approach (2) from https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/32962 with adding the method `order()` to `CryptoProvider`, which allows to have multiple instances of `CryptoProvider` on classpath (Keycloak testsuite still uses the `DefaultCryptoProvider` as before this PR).
